newsitem.title: USA: Mossimo slumps on short-lived problems.
newsitem.headline: Mossimo slumps on short-lived problems.

text.p: Shares of Mossimo Inc tumbled more than 20 percent on Monday when the apparel designer warned of weaker third and fourth quarter earnings.
The Irvine, Calif.-based company said it expects to earn between $0.14 and $0.16 a share in the third quarter compared with a profit of $0.21 a year ago.
The forecast was well below Wall Street estimates, which averaged around $0.26 a share. In the second quarter, Mossimo had net income of $4 million, or $0.26 a share.
The forecast sent shares of Mossimo tumbling to 26-1/4 before recovering to 33-1/2, off 7-1/2, in late afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
The company blamed the weak results on high production costs that hurt its profit margins for men's and women's autumn sportswear collections.
"We had a small problem for the Fall and a development issue that we've got our hands around," Chief Executive Mossimo Giannulli said in a telephone interview.
Mossimo said the higher production costs will also affect its fourth quarter, but have a "substantially less" impact on earnings compared with the third quarter.
Industry analysts said the company may have already repaired its problems, which were caused in large part by the natural growing pains of a newly public company.

"I think this appears to be a one-shot thing that they have addressed," said Brenda Gall, analyst at Merrill Lynch who earlier cut her near-term rating on the company to near-term neutral from accumulate.
Gall said her "conservative" third quarter earnings forecast is $0.15 to $0.18 a share but the company may "possibly" beat that. She expects fourth quarter earnings to be about $0.21 a share.
Gall said Mossimo had too many inexperienced workers handling sourcing while those in charge of product development made far too many expensively priced samples of clothing.
"They were expanding very rapidly ... and they allowed a lot of different people to handle sourcing and their product development procedures were way too expensive," she said.

Recently, Mossimo hired Laura Landis, formerly of Gap Inc's Bannana Republic, to handle centralized sourcing of materials while Anthony Cherbak came aboard as chief financial officer in August to cut costs.
"We didn't know (when Landis was hired) the problems that we had here, in that we had these extreme costs and over- development but we've got our hands around it now," Giannulli said.
Mossimo went public at $18 a share in February 1996.
Despite Monday's selloff, Giannulli remains optimistic for the company's outlook.

"Our sell-throughs have never been better. We're going to have 100 in-stores as opposed to the 50 we were projecting," he said adding that sales for both men's and women's sportswear have already exceeded spring booking expectations.
"On a moving forward basis it is all very positive. It's unfortunate that this situation came up because we were doing so well," he said.
